sense: pay for, provide the money for

terms.grammar: verb phrase: suppeditō, suppeditāre, first conjugation, with the dative of the person or thing paid for
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.42: quae perpetuōs sūmptūs suppeditet
Plaut. As. 4.2.10 (old numbering): luxuriae sūmptūs suppeditāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Suppeditāre is to supply in plenty, frequent in Cicero (Lewis & Short); with sūmptum or sūmptūs, to meet the costs.

evidence: Traupman 311: prīvātō sūmptū, at one’s own expense
terms.comment: Paid for by the state, pūblicō sūmptū (Liv. 40.38.6, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: pecūniae nōn quaerendae sōlum ratiō est, vērum etiam collocandae, quae perpetuōs sūmptūs suppeditet, nec sōlum necessāriōs, sed etiam līberālēs
phrases.english: there is a method not only of making money but of investing it, so that it pays for one’s expenses year after year, the generous ones as well as the necessary

phrases.latin: magnum numerum equitātūs suō sūmptū semper alere et circum sē habēre
phrases.english: that he always kept a large body of cavalry about him at his own expense

sources: Lewis & Short: suppedito · Lewis & Short: sumptus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 311 (at one’s own expense).
